overview.text: The Higgs boson is an elementary particle associated with the Higgs field, a quantum field thought to fill space. It can be understood as a ripple, or excitation, of that field. Interactions with the field give mass to certain fundamental particles, including W and Z bosons, electrons, and quarks; the boson itself is not a particle that simply gives everything its mass. The field and the Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism help explain why the W and Z carriers of the weak force are massive. ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider announced the particle’s discovery in 2012. Its spin is zero, a distinctive property that helped establish its identity.

key_facts.text: The Higgs boson is a ripple, or wave, in the Higgs field; finding it provided evidence for the field.
The Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism describes how interactions with the field give mass to certain fundamental particles, including W and Z bosons.
The photon does not interact with the Higgs field and has no mass.
ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery in 2012; further measurements helped confirm the particle’s spin-zero nature in 2013.
The Higgs mechanism was proposed in 1964 by Peter Higgs, François Englert, and other theorists.
